walkthroughs.body_html:
Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Dialogue Between Religious & Non-Religious Beliefs — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Dialogue Between Religious & Non-Religious Beliefs brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Dialogue Between Religious & Non-Religious Beliefs.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does karma mean in Hindu and Buddhist thought?
options: The principle that actions have moral consequences shaping future experience or rebirth — not fate, but ethical cause and effect built into reality.
Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.
Jihad is the Islamic word for prayer.
Karma is when bad things happen to bad people as punishment.

mcqs.q: What does the term jihad mean in Islam?
options: Jihad means 'holy war' against non-Muslims.
Struggle or striving — the greater jihad is the internal spiritual struggle against sin; the lesser jihad refers to defensive military struggle under strict conditions.
Jihad is the Islamic word for prayer.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Jesus was half God and half human.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
